abstract: Guest essay for the Economic Innovation Group's American Worker Project by Chad Syverson, the George C. Tiao Distinguished Service Professor of Economics at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business and a co-author of the original productivity J-curve paper. Syverson assesses what the aggregate data can and cannot yet say about AI's effect on productivity, and argues the honest answer is that we do not know. He documents that US labor productivity grew about 1.5 percent per year through the 2010s, roughly half its 1995-2004 pace, and that since mid-2022 it has run at roughly 2.2 percent annually. He is deliberately cautious about attributing that acceleration to AI: it began when AI investment was still small relative to the economy, and it coincides with well-documented pandemic-era increases in labor market churn and business formation. He then tests the AI hypothesis cross-sectionally, plotting each sector's change in its contribution to economy-wide productivity growth (2019-25 minus 2007-19) against its employment-weighted Census BTOS 2025 AI adoption rate. The correlation is positive but too weak relative to the number of sectors to rule out chance; excluding retail, which saw a large productivity acceleration despite low adoption, the correlation is more than twice as large and considerably less likely to be chance. On employment, Syverson lays out why productivity growth does not mechanically imply job loss (output is not held fixed, lower costs mean lower prices and higher demand, AI may complement rather than substitute for labor, and slower-growth sectors can absorb displaced workers) and notes that early empirical studies find remarkably little employment effect in either direction. He closes by restating the productivity J-curve and its measurement implication: because complementary intangible investments are expensed rather than capitalized, measured productivity is understated early and overstated later, and on his prior work with Brynjolfsson and Rock those understatement periods can extend well beyond a decade with cumulative mismeasurement in the double-digit percents.
keyFindings: US labor productivity (output per worker-hour) grew about 1.5 percent per year through the 2010s, roughly half its growth rate during the 1995-2004 productivity boom, which ran at nearly 3.0 percent per year.

Since mid-2022, after the pandemic measurement blip unwound, labor productivity has maintained annual growth of about 2.2 percent - a faster-than-2010s trajectory. A sustained move from 1.5 to 2.2 percent would leave GDP per capita 7 percent higher after a decade.

Syverson explicitly declines to attribute the acceleration to AI: it began when AI investment was still small relative to the economy, and its timing matches documented pandemic-era increases in labor market churn and business formation. His stated test is duration - 'the longer the aggregate productivity acceleration continues, the more plausible it is that AI is an important driver.'

Across sectors, the change in a sector's contribution to economy-wide productivity growth (2019-25 minus 2007-19) is positively correlated with its employment-weighted Census BTOS 2025 AI adoption rate, but 'the positive relationship is weak enough, relative to the number of sectors, that one cannot rule out chance as its source.' Dropping retail - a large productivity accelerator with low AI adoption - more than doubles the correlation and makes chance considerably less likely.

On employment: 'At least over the first couple years of its use, AI has had remarkably little employment effect, positive or negative.' Syverson treats this null as informative rather than uninformative about the combined offsetting mechanisms.

Historical calibration for what an AI-driven boom would look like: past general-purpose-technology booms delivered labor productivity growth in excess of 2.5 percent for a decade or longer, raising annual growth by 1 to 1.5 percentage points for a decade or two. Syverson notes the economy absorbed the employment effects of those shifts easily, but that a booster-claimed 5 to 10 percent per year - 'a rate that has not been observed before at an economy-wide level' - could outstrip the economy's absorptive ability.

J-curve restatement from a co-author of the original paper: because complementary intangible investments (worker training, organizational restructuring, business-process redesign) are expensed rather than capitalized, output and therefore productivity are understated during diffusion, then overstated later once that unmeasured intangible capital is in use. On the Brynjolfsson-Rock-Syverson work, understatement periods for other technologies 'could extend well beyond a decade,' with cumulative productivity mismeasurement of double-digit percents.

Syverson's direct answer on AI's current J-curve position: 'Where are we on the AI J-curve now? It is too early to know that with much precision.' He adds that persistently slow measured productivity growth alongside broad AI adoption is not evidence that AI is having no productivity effect.
methodology: Narrative assessment by a leading productivity economist, combining published BLS aggregate labor productivity series with one piece of original descriptive analysis. Figure 1 plots US labor productivity since 2013. Figure 2 is Syverson's own cross-sector scatter: the y-axis is the post-2020 change in a sector's contribution to economy-wide productivity growth, defined as the sector's average annual productivity growth times its average share of total worker-hours, differenced between 2019-25 and 2007-19; the x-axis is the sector's employment-weighted AI adoption rate from the Census BTOS survey administered in 2025 (summarized in Bonney, Breaux, Dinlersoz, Foster, Haltiwanger and Pande, CES Working Paper 26-25). Syverson reports the correlation's sign and significance rather than a fitted coefficient. He focuses on labor productivity for familiarity but states the patterns hold for total factor productivity as well.
qualifiers: Tier 2: an essay for a think tank newsletter (EIG's Agglomerations), not a peer-reviewed paper, though written by a University of Chicago Booth productivity economist and co-author of the canonical J-curve paper. The macro series are BLS data, so the 1.5 and 2.2 percent figures are Tier 1 in provenance; the causal reading is the author's. Figure 2 is descriptive and Syverson is unusually explicit about its fragility - he says taking in all the data one cannot reject chance, and describes the ex-retail specification as 'treading on thin statistical ice' and 'living dangerously.' The ex-retail correlation should therefore never be cited as evidence that AI is raising productivity; it is a conditional robustness note the author himself disowns as a basis for inference. Sector AI adoption is measured in 2025 while the productivity window runs 2019-25, so adoption is a level at the end of the period rather than a measure of exposure across it. The employment null is a synthesis of other studies (Brynjolfsson-Li-Raymond QJE 2025; Humlum-Vestergaard NBER 33777; Yotzov et al. NBER 34836; Bonney et al. NBER 35141; Baslandze et al. forthcoming JF), several already ingested on this site, so it should not be treated as independent corroboration. A commenter on the post raises a substantive critique of footnote 7: Paul David's dynamo account is arguably a threshold story rather than a smooth-lag story, in which factories got nothing from unit drive until the old power system fully depreciated and the plant was rebuilt around it - which would imply a step rather than a curve.
